canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats tool use as selecting, invoking, and using external tools, functions, APIs, models, or code interpreters while solving a task. Most formulations count success as identifying when a tool is needed, choosing the appropriate tool, and generating the required call, code, or arguments, and several also include executing the tool and incorporating returned outputs into later reasoning or answer formation. Most papers describe this as an observable act, though some define it more broadly as a latent capability; a narrower line of work focuses on syntactically and semantically correct API or function calls, while broader formulations include using tool outputs even when they may conflict with the user's request.

Variants. Papers use several close labels for this behavior, especially function calling, tool calling, tool invocation, tool selection, and tool-integrated reasoning. A recurring split is between single-call and multi-call settings, including cases where calls must be coordinated in parallel or through dependencies, and some formulations instead center on writing and executing code or directly interacting with APIs. The behavior is also studied in multi-turn and multimodal settings and in domain-specific workflows such as mathematical, geospatial, clinical, legal, and IT tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure it with 16 instruments. The most common instruments are BFCL and ToolBench, followed by GAIA, API-Bank, and BigCodeBench: papers use these to score correct tool and parameter calls, multi-turn reasoning and tool usage, real-world tool-using scenarios, and code generation with diverse function calls, and some papers adapt API datasets to tool selection. A smaller measurement pattern uses judge-based pairwise comparisons or coherence-style scoring when there is no fixed ground truth.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers connect tool use to 7 constructs, most often Planning, Tool use ability, Reasoning, Grounding, and Instruction following ability. There is no single agreed construct that it reflects: some papers claim Planning or Reasoning cause tool use, while other papers claim a causal relationship from tool use to Planning or Reasoning. Tool use ability is both related to and claimed to cause tool use, Grounding is only related to it, and Instruction following ability is claimed to cause tool use by enabling correct tool-invocation format.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, the prevailing usage treats tool use as selecting, invoking, and using external tools, functions, APIs, models, or code interpreters while solving a task. Most formulations count success as identifying when a tool is needed, choosing the appropriate tool, and generating the required call, code, or arguments, and several also include executing the tool and incorporating returned outputs into later reasoning or answer formation. Most papers describe this as an observable act, though some define it more broadly as a latent capability; a narrower line of work focuses on syntactically and semantically correct API or function calls, while broader formulations include using tool outputs even when they may conflict with the user's request.

characterization_sections.label: Variants.
characterization_sections.text: Papers use several close labels for this behavior, especially function calling, tool calling, tool invocation, tool selection, and tool-integrated reasoning. A recurring split is between single-call and multi-call settings, including cases where calls must be coordinated in parallel or through dependencies, and some formulations instead center on writing and executing code or directly interacting with APIs. The behavior is also studied in multi-turn and multimodal settings and in domain-specific workflows such as mathematical, geospatial, clinical, legal, and IT tasks.

characterization_sections.label: Space of elicitation and scores.
characterization_sections.text: Papers measure it with 16 instruments. The most common instruments are BFCL and ToolBench, followed by GAIA, API-Bank, and BigCodeBench: papers use these to score correct tool and parameter calls, multi-turn reasoning and tool usage, real-world tool-using scenarios, and code generation with diverse function calls, and some papers adapt API datasets to tool selection. A smaller measurement pattern uses judge-based pairwise comparisons or coherence-style scoring when there is no fixed ground truth.

characterization_sections.label: What it is taken as evidence of.
characterization_sections.text: Papers connect tool use to 7 constructs, most often Planning, Tool use ability, Reasoning, Grounding, and Instruction following ability. There is no single agreed construct that it reflects: some papers claim Planning or Reasoning cause tool use, while other papers claim a causal relationship from tool use to Planning or Reasoning. Tool use ability is both related to and claimed to cause tool use, Grounding is only related to it, and Instruction following ability is claimed to cause tool use by enabling correct tool-invocation format.
